title: Eliphaz's Counsel: Appeal to God and Accept His Discipline
summary: Eliphaz continues, warning that resentment destroys the fool and that trouble is the common lot of humanity. He urges Job to appeal to God, who does great and unsearchable things, lifts up the lowly, and frustrates the crafty. Calling Job's suffering the discipline of the Almighty, he promises that if Job accepts it, God will heal him, protect him, and give him a long and prosperous life.
story: This chapter completes Eliphaz's first speech, begun in chapter 4. There he argued that the innocent do not perish and that no one is righteous before God. Here he turns to advice. His counsel sounds pious, and many of his lines could stand in the Psalms or Proverbs. But underneath it is the same assumption: Job's suffering must be deserved, so he should accept correction and all will be well. Job will reply in chapters 6 and 7, rejecting both the diagnosis and the cure. The rest of the dialogue will largely repeat and sharpen the positions laid out in these first speeches.
historical:
The chapter reflects the agricultural and pastoral life of the ancient Near East. Eliphaz speaks of harvests, thorns, rain on the fields, famine, war, and wild beasts, dangers that could destroy a family's livelihood in a single season. His promise of a secure tent, many descendants, and death in old age like a sheaf gathered in season describes the blessings every family in that world hoped for, and the losses Job has already suffered.

Verse 4 mentions the gate, where the elders of a town sat to settle disputes and administer justice. To be crushed in the gate without a defender meant to lose one's case in court with no one to speak for you, a fate that could strip a family of property and standing.
cultural:
Eliphaz's opening question, to which of the holy ones will you turn, assumes a belief in heavenly beings who might intercede for people. His point is that no such intercessor will help Job if he is guilty. Later Job will long for exactly such a mediator (9:33; 16:19).

The proverb in verse 7, that man is born to trouble as surely as sparks fly upward, uses an image from daily life: the sparks rising from a fire. The Hebrew literally says the sons of Resheph fly upward. Resheph was the name of a Canaanite god of plague and fire, but here the word is used poetically for flames or sparks, much as English uses mythological names in ordinary speech. The idea of discipline in verse 17 comes from the family: a father corrects a son he loves. The wisdom tradition applied this to God's dealings with his people, and Proverbs 3:11-12 says something very similar.
literary: Eliphaz's speech moves from warning (verses 1-7) to advice (verse 8) to a hymn of God's power (verses 9-16) and ends with a beatitude and a list of promises (verses 17-26). The hymn in verses 9-16 uses the pattern of praise found in the Psalms, describing what God does: gives rain, lifts the lowly, thwarts the crafty, saves the needy. The numerical saying in verse 19, six calamities and seven, is a common Hebrew device meaning a full number of troubles. The promises of verses 19-26 pile up images of security. The speech ends with a claim of authority: we have investigated, it is true, hear it. This confidence is exactly what the book will call into question.

outline.t: The fool's end and humanity's trouble
Appeal to the God who does great things

doctrines.note: Eliphaz's hymn describes God's power over nature and human affairs: he gives rain, lifts the lowly, and frustrates the schemes of the crafty. These are true descriptions of God, found throughout Scripture.

Eliphaz sees suffering as discipline meant to correct. Scripture does teach that God disciplines his children, but the book of Job shows that not all suffering is discipline for sin, and that treating it that way can wound the innocent.
Paul quotes verse 13 in 1 Corinthians 3:19. The friends' words can contain true wisdom even when their application to Job is wrong, which is part of what makes the book demanding to read.

words.note: Musar, discipline, correction, instruction. The word is central to Proverbs, where it describes the training a father gives a son. Eliphaz calls Job's suffering the discipline of the Almighty. Scripture affirms such discipline, but Job's case shows it is not the only explanation of suffering.

Shaddai, the Almighty. It is one of the oldest names for God in the Old Testament, used with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Genesis 17:1). It appears more often in Job than in any other book, fitting the book's patriarchal setting. Its exact origin is debated.

Amal, trouble, toil, misery. Man is born to trouble, Eliphaz says. The same word appears in 3:10, where Job laments that he was not spared trouble, and it runs through Ecclesiastes to describe the labor of life under the sun.

Berit, covenant. Eliphaz promises that Job will be in covenant with the stones of the field, a poetic picture of harmony with creation, when even the ground and wild animals are at peace with him. It is one of the rare uses of the word in Job.

christ: Eliphaz says that God “wounds, but He also binds” and that his hands also heal (Job 5:18). The New Testament finds this pattern fulfilled in Christ, of whom Isaiah wrote that “by His stripes we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). The link is thematic. Paul quotes Eliphaz's words about God catching the wise in their craftiness (1 Corinthians 3:19) to show that God's wisdom, displayed in the message of the cross, overturns human cleverness. Hebrews 12:5-6 also speaks of the Lord's discipline of those he loves, drawing on Proverbs 3. But the book of Job adds a vital warning: discipline is not the explanation for every suffering, and Christ himself suffered not for his own sin but for others.
questions: Eliphaz's advice sounds pious but misses Job's situation. How can you tell when true words are being used in the wrong way?
Eliphaz says God wounds and heals. Where have you experienced something painful that later became a source of healing or growth?
Eliphaz promises that if Job accepts discipline, everything will be restored. Why is it dangerous to promise sufferers that their troubles will end if they respond correctly?
